blocks.content: A resource allocation graph is a formal drawing that shows exactly which process is holding which resource, and exactly which process is waiting for which resource, across an entire system at one moment in time. It turns an abstract, hard to hold in your head situation into a small picture made of circles, boxes, and arrows. Once you can read one of these graphs fluently, deciding whether a system is deadlocked stops being a guess and becomes a mechanical check.

This chapter is entirely about learning that picture. We will look at the two kinds of nodes and the two kinds of edges that make up the notation, build a small example graph one edge at a time, and then apply the single rule that tells you whether a cycle in the graph actually means deadlock. By the end you should be able to draw a correct graph from a plain description of a scenario and read off the answer with confidence.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759254-853420684.png
1. Why This Graph Notation Exists

Earlier in this module you met deadlock through short verbal descriptions and small code snippets, such as two threads each holding one lock and waiting for the other. That works for two threads, but real systems have dozens of processes and many kinds of resources, and a paragraph of prose quickly becomes impossible to follow. A resource allocation graph solves this by giving every process, every resource, every request, and every assignment a fixed, unambiguous symbol.

The graph is not just a teaching tool either. Anyone reasoning about a suspected deadlock, whether in an exam question or a real production incident, benefits from sketching the exact same picture, because it forces you to state precisely who holds what and who is waiting for what, rather than reasoning loosely in your head.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: A resource allocation graph is a diagram of processes and resources connected by request and assignment edges, and its main use is deciding whether the system it describes is deadlocked.
2. The Two Types of Nodes: Processes and Resources
blocks.text: 2. The Two Types of Nodes: Processes and Resources

blocks.content: Every resource allocation graph has exactly two kinds of nodes, and telling them apart at a glance is the first skill to build. A process node is drawn as a circle, and it represents one running or waiting program, such as a specific thread or a specific application instance. A resource node is drawn as a box, and it represents one type of resource that processes compete for, such as a printer, a lock, or a pool of database connections.

The box for a resource carries one extra piece of information that the circle for a process never needs, which is how many identical instances of that resource actually exist. A printer with a single physical unit is drawn as a box with one small dot inside it. A pool of two identical database connections is drawn as a box with two small dots inside it, one dot for each interchangeable unit. This dot count turns out to be the single most important detail in the entire notation, because it is exactly what decides whether a cycle later in the graph is dangerous or harmless.

blocks.alt: The Two Types of Nodes: Processes and Resources

3. The Two Types of Edges: Request and Assignment
blocks.text: 3. The Two Types of Edges: Request and Assignment

blocks.content: A request edge always starts at a process circle and points at a resource box. It means exactly one thing, that the process has asked for that resource and has not yet received it, so it is currently sitting and waiting. The arrow points toward the resource because that is where the process is looking, at the thing it wants next.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759254-975038420.png
blocks.alt: The Two Types of Edges: Request and Assignment

blocks.content: An assignment edge always starts at a resource box and points at a process circle. It means the opposite kind of thing, that the resource, or one instance of it, has already been handed out and is currently held by that process. The arrow points toward the process because that is where the resource physically ended up.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759465-130565754.png
blocks.alt: The Two Types of Edges: Request and Assignment

blocks.content: Getting the direction backward is the most common mistake beginners make with this notation, and it matters enormously, because a graph read with reversed arrows can make a perfectly healthy system look deadlocked, or hide a real deadlock entirely. A simple habit fixes this: a circle can only ever be the start of a request edge or the end of an assignment edge, never the other way around.

{"headers":["Aspect","Request edge","Assignment edge"],"rows":[["Drawn from","A process (circle)","A resource (box)"],["Drawn to","A resource (box)","A process (circle)"],["Meaning","The process is currently waiting to acquire that resource","The resource is currently allocated to and held by that process"],["Arrow direction","Circle to box","Box to circle"]]}

blocks.title: Direction rule of thumb
blocks.content: If the arrow leaves a circle, it is a request. If the arrow leaves a box, it is an assignment. The shape the arrow starts from tells you everything.
4. Building a Complete Graph Step by Step
blocks.text: 4. Building a Complete Graph Step by Step

blocks.content: Graphs are easiest to trust once you have watched one grow, so let us build a small, realistic one edge at a time. Picture a laptop running a photo editing process, call it P1, and a background backup process, call it P2. The machine has exactly one physical printer, call it R1, and it also has a small pool of database connections used to save progress, call it R2.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759465-359144033.png
blocks.alt: Building a Complete Graph Step by Step

blocks.content: At this starting instant nothing has happened yet, so the graph has four nodes and zero edges, as shown above. Now say the editing process finishes a print job setup and is granted the printer. That adds our first edge, an assignment edge from R1 to P1, since the resource now points at whoever holds it.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759465-498377683.png
blocks.alt: Building a Complete Graph Step by Step

blocks.content: Next, while still holding the printer, the editing process tries to save its progress and asks for a database connection from R2. Since that connection has not been granted yet, this adds a request edge from P1 to R2, a circle pointing at a box.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759466-977329119.png
blocks.alt: Building a Complete Graph Step by Step

blocks.content: Meanwhile the backup process has already been given one of the database connections, so we add an assignment edge from R2 to P2. And then, to finish its backup, the backup process tries to print a summary report, which means it now requests the printer, adding a request edge from P2 to R1.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759466-2980414.png
blocks.alt: Building a Complete Graph Step by Step

blocks.content: /engineering/library/os/images/1785408759466-564927389.png
blocks.alt: Building a Complete Graph Step by Step

blocks.content: Look closely at the completed picture. Following the arrows from P1, you go to R2, then to P2, then to R1, and then straight back to P1. That closed loop is called a cycle, and spotting it is the entire reason this notation exists. Whether that cycle actually means the system is stuck is the question the rest of this chapter answers.
5. The Cycle Rule: The Single Most Important Idea
blocks.text: 5. The Cycle Rule: The Single Most Important Idea

blocks.content: Here is the rule that everything else in this topic builds toward, and it comes in two halves. If a resource allocation graph contains no cycle at all, the system it describes is definitely not deadlocked, no exceptions. Every process can eventually get what it needs, because there is no closed loop of waiting for the request chain to run into.

The second half needs more care. If the graph does contain a cycle, deadlock is only guaranteed when every resource type inside that cycle has exactly one instance. When a resource type inside the cycle has more than one instance, the cycle alone does not settle the question, because a free instance elsewhere might let one of the waiting processes proceed and unwind the whole chain. We will walk through both situations concretely in the next section.

A resource allocation graph is checked for cycles the same way any directed graph is, with a depth first search that watches for a node being revisited while it is still on the current path. You rarely need to trace this by hand once a graph is small enough to draw, but it is worth seeing once, since it is exactly the tool detection algorithms use under the hood.

blocks.title: The rule in one line
blocks.content: No cycle means no deadlock, guaranteed. A cycle where every resource in it has a single instance means deadlock, guaranteed. A cycle where some resource in it has multiple instances means maybe, and you have to look closer.
6. Single Instance vs Multiple Instances: Two Worked Examples
blocks.text: 6. Single Instance vs Multiple Instances: Two Worked Examples

blocks.content: Case one: every resource has a single instance
blocks.text: Case one: every resource has a single instance

blocks.content: Return to the completed printer and database connection graph from section four, and assume for now that the database connection resource R2, like the printer R1, has only one instance total, perhaps because it is a single exclusive connection to an old legacy system that cannot be shared. Under that assumption the cycle from P1 to R2 to P2 to R1 and back to P1 is a genuine deadlock.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759466-78718009.png
blocks.alt: Case one: every resource has a single instance

blocks.content: Walk through why neither process can ever move again. P1 is holding the printer and waiting for the one and only database connection, which is entirely in the hands of P2. P2 is holding that connection and waiting for the printer, which is entirely in the hands of P1. Neither one will ever release what it holds, because releasing happens only after finishing, and finishing needs the thing the other process is sitting on. This is deadlock in the strictest sense, confirmed purely by reading the graph.
Case two: a resource in the cycle has multiple instances
blocks.text: Case two: a resource in the cycle has multiple instances

blocks.content: Now change exactly one fact. Suppose the database connection resource R2 is actually a small pool with two identical connections rather than one, which is the far more common setup in real systems. The graph looks almost identical, R2 still shows an assignment edge to P2 and P1 still shows a request edge pointing at R2, except the box for R2 now carries two dots instead of one, and only one of those two connections is currently checked out.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759467-785627640.png
blocks.alt: Case two: a resource in the cycle has multiple instances

blocks.content: Trace what actually happens this time. P1 requests a database connection, and the resource manager sees that R2 has a second, unused instance sitting free, so it hands that free connection straight to P1 without making it wait at all. P1 finishes its save and releases both the connection and, shortly after, the printer. P2 then acquires the now free printer, finishes its report, and releases its own connection. Every process eventually completes, so despite the cycle looking exactly the same shape on paper, this system was never actually deadlocked.

{"headers":["Situation","Cycle present","Every resource in the cycle has one instance","Deadlock guaranteed"],"rows":[["No cycle anywhere in the graph","No","Not applicable","No, the system is definitely not deadlocked"],["Cycle exists, every resource type in it has exactly one instance","Yes","Yes","Yes, deadlock is guaranteed"],["Cycle exists, at least one resource type in it has multiple instances","Yes","No","Not necessarily, progress may still be possible"]]}

blocks.title: Do not stop at the cycle
blocks.content: Finding a cycle is only half the job. Before declaring deadlock, always check the instance count of every resource type inside that cycle, since a single resource with a spare instance is enough to break the whole chain.
7. From Resource Allocation Graph to Wait For Graph
blocks.text: 7. From Resource Allocation Graph to Wait For Graph

blocks.content: The sibling Detection and Recovery topic in this module introduces a simpler picture called a wait for graph, and it is worth seeing exactly how the two relate. A wait for graph keeps only the process circles and throws away every resource box, leaving direct process to process edges that mean one process is waiting on another.

You can build a wait for graph mechanically from a resource allocation graph by chasing two edges at a time and collapsing them into one. Think of a request edge as a forward pointer that tells you which resource a process is looking at next, and think of the matching assignment edge on that resource as a backward pointer that tells you who is actually holding it. Follow the forward pointer from P1 to R1, then follow the backward pointer from R1 onward to P2, and draw a single direct edge from P1 to P2 in the simplified graph, skipping the resource entirely.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759467-319236344.png
blocks.alt: From Resource Allocation Graph to Wait For Graph

blocks.content: This simplification is convenient specifically because a plain cycle check on a wait for graph is enough to prove deadlock, but only when every resource in the system has a single instance, since that is exactly the case where the resource allocation graph cycle rule and the wait for graph cycle rule agree. Once resources can have multiple instances, the wait for graph throws away the very detail, the dot count, that the full resource allocation graph exists to preserve, so systems with pooled resources need the richer picture or a dedicated detection algorithm instead.
8. Why This Notation Is Genuinely Useful
blocks.text: 8. Why This Notation Is Genuinely Useful

blocks.content: It is easy to file this away as a purely academic diagram meant for exam questions, but the same picture earns its keep in real debugging. When several threads in a production system appear frozen, sketching a resource allocation graph from the actual locks and threads involved turns a vague feeling of being stuck into a precise, checkable claim that a teammate can verify or challenge.

The notation is also valuable simply as a shared vocabulary. Saying a system is deadlocked because of a cycle is far less useful than pointing at a specific circle, a specific box, and a specific arrow and saying exactly why. Two engineers looking at the same graph will always agree on what it shows, which is rarely true of a purely verbal description of a complex waiting situation.
9. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle
blocks.text: 9. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle

blocks.content: A short list of mistakes accounts for almost every wrong answer involving this notation. Drawing an edge backward is the most frequent one, followed closely by mixing up which edge type is which, and then, most dangerously, spotting any cycle at all and declaring deadlock without ever checking how many instances of each resource in that cycle actually exist.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759467-811188619.png
blocks.alt: Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle

blocks.content: ["Drawing an assignment edge from a process to a resource instead of from the resource to the process, which reverses its entire meaning.","Labeling a request edge as an assignment edge or the reverse, especially when redrawing a graph quickly from memory under time pressure.","Declaring deadlock the moment a cycle appears without checking whether every resource type inside that cycle has only one instance.","Forgetting that a single resource box can represent several interchangeable instances, and drawing it as if it were always exactly one."]
items: Drawing an assignment edge from a process to a resource instead of from the resource to the process, which reverses its entire meaning.
Labeling a request edge as an assignment edge or the reverse, especially when redrawing a graph quickly from memory under time pressure.
Declaring deadlock the moment a cycle appears without checking whether every resource type inside that cycle has only one instance.
Forgetting that a single resource box can represent several interchangeable instances, and drawing it as if it were always exactly one.

blocks.content: Interviewers who ask about deadlocks often describe a small scenario out loud, a couple of processes and a couple of resources, and expect you to reconstruct the picture on a whiteboard. Being able to place the circles and boxes correctly, draw each request and assignment edge in the right direction, spot any cycle, and then correctly state whether that cycle proves deadlock or merely suggests it, is exactly the skill this chapter has been building.
Draw the graph first, then answer the question. A correct resource allocation graph turns a deadlock question into something you can read the answer off of, rather than something you have to guess.
